title: A New Engine of Development
gist: Michael Beckley documents the end of the convergence boom with hard numbers — developing economies paid foreign creditors $741 billion more than they received from 2022-24, Chinese lending collapsed from $87bn in 2016 to under $4bn in 2021, export employment fell 45 million between 2007 and 2018 — and argues the only durable replacement engine is trading rich-world market access, capital and legal visas for reliable supply and trained workers, built outward from existing footholds rather than greenfield industrial parks.

themes.theme: The four growth accelerators are all failing

insights.claim: The rich-poor income gap narrowed from over 8-to-1 in 1991 to 5-to-1 by 2016 not because poor countries solved domestic problems but because the open world economy supplied what they lacked — customers, production systems, capital and state capacity — and all four supports are now giving way.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Convergence was exogenous, not earned — remove the external supports and EM growth premia over DM structurally compress, which is already happening.
insights.quote: The post-Cold War convergence boom was a historical anomaly.
insights.locator: The post-Cold War convergence boom

insights.claim: From 1991 to 2016 poor countries grew twice as fast as rich ones — nearly three times as fast including China and India — with incomes tripling, child mortality and conflict deaths roughly halving, and the number of democracies doubling.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline that has now reversed; the EM growth-differential trade that underpinned two decades of allocation no longer has its structural driver.
insights.locator: The contrast between Bangladesh’s boom

insights.claim: All 72 countries the World Bank classifies as low- or lower-middle-income collectively consume only one-quarter as much as the United States, so external demand is not a supplement but a prerequisite for their growth.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Quantifies why domestic-demand-led development is not available to poor countries — market access from rich countries is the binding variable.
insights.quote: All 72 countries currently classified by the World Bank as low- or lower-middle-income collectively consume only one-quarter as much as the United States.
insights.locator: First, poor countries are losing the foreign customers

insights.claim: Discriminatory trade measures affecting poor countries have risen 72 percent since 2016, and in 2025 U.S. tariffs on the world's least developed countries averaged twice those on developed economies.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Trade policy is now actively regressive by income level — a quantified headwind for frontier-market export earnings and currency stability.
insights.quote: In 2025, U.S. tariffs on the world’s least developed countries averaged twice those on developed economies.
insights.locator: But now markets are closing

insights.claim: China produces a third of the world's manufactured output — more than three times its 2004 share — its trade surplus has tripled since 2018, and it still captures nearly two-thirds of global value added in low-skill exports from poor countries including apparel, textiles, leather and footwear.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: China is not vacating the bottom rungs as it climbs — the classic development ladder is blocked, which caps the upside of 'China+1' relocation stories.
insights.quote: Poorer countries may stitch the final shirt or shoe, but China increasingly supplies the fabric, yarn, trimmings, and other inputs—and retains much of the income, employment, and know-how.
insights.locator: China, meanwhile, is climbing the manufacturing ladder

insights.claim: Industrial robots per 10,000 manufacturing workers worldwide more than doubled between 2016 and 2023 while multinationals concentrate production in established hubs closer to rich-country markets.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Automation plus nearshoring structurally erodes the cheap-labor arbitrage — bearish for frontier-market industrialization theses, bullish for robotics and nearshore hubs.
insights.locator: Now, even those narrow roles are disappearing

insights.claim: Export-related employment roughly halved in some poor countries since the 2000s, falling by 45 million between 2007 and 2018 alone, with many remaining jobs vulnerable to automation.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: A 45-million-job loss is the scale of the employment gap driving migration pressure and political instability in the global south.
insights.quote: altogether falling by 45 million between 2007 and 2018 alone
insights.locator: Since the 2000s, export-related employment

insights.claim: Poor countries are losing factory jobs at roughly one-twentieth the income level at which rich countries shed theirs, long before white-collar jobs can absorb workers — leaving 60 to 80 percent of the working population in the informal sector.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Premature deindustrialization locks in low productivity and thin tax bases — a structural ceiling on frontier sovereign credit quality.
insights.quote: Many poor countries are deindustrializing before they get a chance to develop.
insights.locator: Second, many poor countries are deindustrializing

insights.claim: Chinese lending to developing countries collapsed from $87 billion in 2016 to under $4 billion in 2021, after China had extended more than $800 billion in new loans between 2000 and 2017.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: A 95%+ collapse in the marginal lender of the 2010s explains the EM infrastructure funding gap and the surge in distressed sovereign situations.
insights.quote: Chinese lending fell from $87 billion in 2016 to under $4 billion in 2021.
insights.locator: Then the flow reversed

insights.claim: From 2022 to 2024 developing economies paid foreign creditors $741 billion more than they received in new disbursements, and by 2023 one-quarter of developing economies had lost bond market access.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Net negative transfers of this size are a self-reinforcing contraction — expect more defaults, restructurings and IMF programs across the frontier universe.
insights.quote: From 2022 to 2024, they paid foreign creditors $741 billion more than they received in new disbursements.
insights.locator: Then the flow reversed

insights.claim: Interest payments have quadrupled over the past decade, pushing more than half of poor countries into debt distress or high risk of it, with some 3.4 billion people living in countries that spend more on interest than on health or education.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Debt service is crowding out the human capital spending that would generate future growth — the mechanism by which the debt trap becomes permanent.
insights.locator: Interest payments have quadrupled

insights.claim: Beckley argues future borrowing must be tied to projects that can support themselves or unlock real business, with better debt and loan disclosure, or debt relief simply restarts the cycle of borrow, default, forgive, repeat.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Disclosure requirements and revenue-linked conditionality are the likely direction of future sovereign lending architecture — relevant to how new EM debt gets structured.
insights.quote: Otherwise, debt relief simply restarts the cycle: borrow, default, forgive, repeat.
insights.locator: Finance should follow the same logic

insights.claim: Eight of the 10 largest OECD donors cut aid in 2024, the Trump administration terminated 86 percent of USAID programs, and U.N. peacekeepers are down 60 percent from their peak of 125,000 in 2015.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: A simultaneous withdrawal of aid and security provision raises the probability of state failure events, with knock-on refugee, commodity and shipping disruption.
insights.quote: The Trump administration terminated 86 percent of U.S. Agency for International Development programs, and the number of U.N. peacekeepers has fallen 60 percent from its peak.
insights.locator: But much of this global aid industry bypassed

insights.claim: In 2020 recipient governments and local organizations directly managed less than 9 percent of U.S. aid — foreign contractors delivered services then left with the money and expertise, meaning decades of aid built little local capacity.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Explains why the aid drawdown is producing rapid deterioration — there was no accumulated local capability to absorb the shock.
insights.quote: In 2020, recipient governments and local organizations directly managed less than 9 percent of U.S. aid.
insights.locator: But much of this global aid industry bypassed

insights.claim: Thirteen poor-country democracies have collapsed into autocracy — a quarter of their ranks — while battle deaths have more than doubled, nearly one-third of Africa's 54 countries are at war, and global under-5 child deaths were projected to rise in 2025 for the first time in decades.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: The development reversal is already producing measurable political and humanitarian regression — a leading indicator of commodity supply disruption and migration surges.
insights.locator: Now, the era of easy growth has ended

insights.claim: Georgia's post-2003 Rose Revolution government raised tax revenue from 14 to 25 percent of GDP within four years by cutting taxes from 21 to seven, lowering rates, dismissing corrupt officials, replacing the police and enforcing remaining rules.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Proof that fiscal capacity can improve dramatically in four years with narrow focus — a template for assessing reform credibility in frontier sovereigns.
insights.locator: Georgia shows how quickly basic state capacity

themes.theme: Foothold strategy: build outward, not greenfield

insights.claim: Ethiopia borrowed $1 billion mainly for six industrial parks that by mid-2021 employed only about 90,000 people in a country adding 2 million workers a year, while carrying nearly $500 million in scheduled interest — and then defaulted.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: The canonical failure case for debt-financed greenfield industrial policy — a warning applicable to current African and South Asian special economic zone programs.
insights.locator: One generation later, Ethiopia tried to climb

insights.claim: Bangladesh's garment exports rose more than a thousandfold from barely $30 million in the mid-1980s to over $40 billion by 2022, employing roughly 4 million people, lifting average income from under $300 to about $2,600 since 1990 — enabled by EU tariff abolition, U.S. quotas on rivals, and Daewoo training the first manager cohort.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Shows the specific policy inputs — preferential access plus competitor restriction plus foreign management transfer — that produced the last great takeoff, none of which is available today.
insights.locator: In the mid-1980s, Bangladesh seemed an unlikely candidate

insights.claim: The correct strategy is to build outward from what already works — a working mine, factory cluster, seaport or city — removing specific bottlenecks like unreliable electricity, slow customs, missing cold storage or supplier financing, rather than building capacity before customers exist.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: A screening rule for development investments: demand-first beats supply-first, which favors brownfield debottlenecking projects over new-zone megaprojects.
insights.quote: The safer strategy is to build outward from what already works by removing the specific barriers that keep existing firms from growing.
insights.locator: The second group lacks a scarce resource

insights.claim: Vietnam's share of world trade rose from 0.1 percent in 1996 to 1.5 percent in 2023, making it the 19th-largest exporter, though foreign firms still produce nearly three-quarters of its exports.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Quantifies the last successful supply-chain-driven ascent and its dependency profile — useful as the benchmark against which India or Mexico's current attempts are measured.
insights.locator: Vietnam pushed the same process further

insights.claim: Botswana's model — national control of mineral rights, a 50-50 joint venture with De Beers for expertise, and diamond revenues flowing to the treasury rather than elites, invested by a well-paid civil service — is the clearest precedent for converting resource leverage into lasting development.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: The specific institutional conditions under which resource deals create national value — a diligence checklist for evaluating current critical-minerals agreements.
insights.locator: The logic, however, is not new

insights.claim: Strategic leverage from minerals or chokepoints is temporary and should be traded for durable assets — railways, ports, reliable power, worker training, local processing or market access — via concrete, enforceable bargains such as guaranteed mineral supply in exchange for electricity and transport infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Defines the deal structure resource-rich states will increasingly demand — raising the infrastructure capex attached to offtake agreements for Western buyers.
insights.locator: For the first group, today’s fractured global economy

insights.claim: Morocco is combining European proximity, modern ports, trade agreements, an established auto industry and key mineral deposits to attract EV and battery-materials investment, while Zambia is leveraging copper demand and interest in the Lobito Corridor.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Two named, live test cases for the resource-leverage-to-capability conversion — concrete places where Western supply-chain diversification capital is actually landing.
insights.locator: Several countries are testing this strategy now

themes.theme: The demographic bargain: workers for capital

insights.claim: By 2050 many rich economies will lose 15 to 40 percent of their populations aged 25-49 while Africa adds an estimated 1 billion people — an imbalance that could fuel either growth or instability.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: The single largest structural factor-supply mismatch of the century; whichever side of it a country sits on determines its growth constraint.
insights.quote: By 2050, many rich economies will lose 15 to 40 percent of their populations between ages 25 and 49, while Africa will add an estimated 1 billion people.
insights.locator: The stakes are enormous

insights.claim: Roughly 12 to 15 million Africans enter the labor market each year but only around 3 million formal jobs are created, and in 2024 nearly half of Africans surveyed across 24 countries said they had considered emigrating.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: A 4-to-1 job shortfall with half the population contemplating emigration is the quantified source of future European and Gulf migration pressure and political risk.
insights.quote: Roughly 12 million to 15 million Africans enter the labor market each year, but only around 3 million formal jobs are created.
insights.locator: The stakes are enormous

insights.claim: Africa now has more conflicts than at any point since at least 1946 and displaced people on the continent more than tripled between 2009 and 2023 to 32.5 million — a continent adding a billion people amid spreading violence could produce far greater shocks than Syria.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Frames a plausible tail scenario of migration shock several times the 2015 European crisis — with corresponding European political and fiscal consequences.
insights.locator: The consequences become more severe

insights.claim: The proposed bargain is transactional and narrow: rich countries provide market access, financing and legal work visas; poor countries provide reliable supplies, targeted worker training and migration-enforcement cooperation — with each benefit tied to a concrete obligation.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Describes the politically feasible form future development policy will take — conditional bilateral deals, not multilateral aid, which changes who captures the flows.
insights.quote: The point is to tie each benefit to a concrete obligation on the other side.
insights.locator: The practical agenda should be narrow

insights.claim: Digital services are a tariff-free workaround because U.S. tariffs apply to goods not services — a worker in Nairobi or Dhaka can serve a New York or London firm without emigrating or shipping through a tariff wall — though the jobs require education, reliable power, broadband and language skills and will not absorb workers at factory scale.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Services trade is the growth channel least exposed to the tariff regime — favors countries and firms with broadband, power and English-language capability.
insights.quote: U.S. tariffs apply to imported goods, not services
insights.locator: Digital services offer another route

insights.claim: Poland, poorer per person than Botswana in 1991 and now roughly as rich as Japan on a purchasing-power basis, demonstrates that market integration with richer consumers is the decisive engine rather than aid or investment alone.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Market access dominates all other development inputs — the strongest argument for preferential trade arrangements over aid budgets.
insights.locator: Poland shows how powerful that access can be

insights.claim: Legal migration should be limited, targeted to occupations with genuine shortages such as nurses, caregivers, electricians, builders and farm workers, largely temporary, with employers rather than taxpayers bearing recruitment and training costs.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Predicts the design of politically survivable migration programs — employer-sponsored, occupation-specific and temporary, shifting costs onto labor-short industries.
insights.locator: Trade and investment, however, will still leave millions

insights.claim: Rich countries will not rebuild collapsed states — the interventions that ended wars in Sierra Leone and Liberia required years of troops, money and political attention that few governments would commit today — so the realistic policy is damage control.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Assume state collapse goes uncontained going forward — raising the persistence and geographic spread of conflict-driven commodity and shipping disruptions.
insights.locator: Most jobs must still be created in poor countries

insights.claim: Supporting front-line neighbor states may do more to contain a war's fallout than funding a disintegrated government — during the Syrian war refugees equaled roughly one-seventh of Jordan's and one-quarter of Lebanon's populations, and by September 2015 each had taken in more Syrians than all of Europe combined.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Front-line states are where marginal aid dollars have most leverage — and where fiscal and social stress concentrates first in any new conflict.
insights.locator: If the state falls apart anyway

insights.claim: State collapse exports refugees, epidemics, piracy and violence across borders and disrupts trade routes, so outside powers should focus on keeping local disasters from becoming global catastrophes — as foreign assistance did in the 2014-16 West African Ebola outbreak.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Containment-focused intervention is the new baseline — expect episodic, narrow crisis responses rather than sustained stabilization, leaving longer-duration disruptions.
insights.locator: The alternative is damage control

insights.claim: Advising poor countries to copy East Asia is useless because that model depended on a unique Cold War bargain in which the U.S. protected allies, financed their growth and opened its market to build anti-communist bastions — a bargain that no longer exists.
insights.speaker: Michael Beckley
insights.so_what: Invalidates the most commonly cited development playbook — country-selection for EM investment should weight current bargaining assets, not historical analogies.
insights.quote: Some economists still advise poor countries to copy East Asia. They might as well tell them to invent fusion.
insights.locator: The first rule for development in this new era
